subject: Climate & Environment
title: Climate Models and Predictions
description: Learn Climate Models and Predictions in one minute.

hook.text: In the 1960s, scientists built the first computer models to simulate Earth's climate.

buildup.text: They split the atmosphere into a 3D grid and calculated physics for each cell step by step.

discovery.text: Early models predicted about 1°C of warming by 2020. Reality matched remarkably well.

twist.text: Critics said models were unreliable. Decades later, their forecasts keep proving accurate.

climax.text: Modern models use millions of grid cells running on the world's fastest supercomputers.

punchline.text: The computers warned us. We didn't listen fast enough.

quiz.question: How accurate were early climate models in predicting warming by 2020?

details.summary: Climate models are complex computer simulations that divide the atmosphere, ocean, and land into millions of grid cells and calculate physical processes at each one. They have accurately predicted warming trends since the 1970s and are the primary tool for projecting future climate.
details.whyItMatters: Models are the basis for every IPCC scenario and climate policy target. Understanding their strengths and limitations is key to interpreting climate projections.
takeaways: Modern models simulate atmosphere, ocean, ice, land, and biology
They have accurately predicted warming observed over the past 50 years
Uncertainty comes mainly from future emission choices, not physics errors

faq.question: How accurate have climate models been?
faq.answer: Multiple studies show that models from the 1970s through 2000s predicted global warming within a few tenths of a degree of what was actually observed. The physics is robust; the main uncertainty is what humans will emit in the future.

faq.question: Why do different climate models give different answers?
faq.answer: Models differ in resolution, cloud physics, ocean mixing, and other parameterizations. Running multiple models and averaging results, called an ensemble, improves confidence. The spread among models gives a measure of scientific uncertainty.
